full_judgment:
Mr. A.H.M. Shamsuddin Choudhury, J.: The Application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, which yielded the present rule, issued on 17.11.2001, sprang from an order dated 18.10.2001 passed by the learned 3rd court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka allowing the Arbitration Miscellaneous case no. 41 of 1999. By the said order the learned Subordinate Judge directed the parties to provide with the names of their choice of Arbitrators by 1.11.2001. 

 2. Alleged facts, as relied on by the opposite party, who was the petitioner in the said miscellaneous case in the court below (hereinafter referred to as the opposite party,) in prosecuting his said miscellaneous case are reconstructed below in precise from. 

 3. The opposite party successfully respondent to a tender invitation, which the petitioner herein, (the opposite party in the court below), henceforth referred to as the petitioner, floated, on 31.1.96 seeking bids 'from contractors for site development of its staff quarter premises at Sylhet for an estimated costs of Tk. 14,45,000/00. A work order was duly issued to the opposite party on 12.1.1997. The opposite party submitted banks guarantee for Tk. 1.38.384/00 and duly afixe his signature on the contract. It was stipulated in the contract that the work would be completed within four months from the date of issuance of the work order. The opposite party witnessed a number of deep holes within the site precincts when he, along with the engineer of the petitioners Sylhet office, visited the site on 21.1.97. The petitioner, at that stage, minded to fill in those holes, but the filling in process accounted for an enormous length of time. Consequently the opposite party had to remain in the site for a period of twelve months, whereas the 'work could very well be completed within the stipulated four months period, had the holes been stuffed earlier. The petitioner acted arbitrarily in granting work order some seven months and twenty days after the receipt of communication from the opposite party and deviated from its earlier verbal promise of enhancing the cost for the work. The petitioner improperly enhanced the bank guarantee without giving the opposite party any opportunity to show cause which act damaged the opposite party's business goodwill computed in terms of money at Tk. 2500000.00 at least. The opposite party sustained loss on several other counts as well and by accumulating claims for compensation etc under different heads laid a demand to the petitioner for a total amount of Tk. 5663803.0'0. Despite recurring request the petitioner gave no heed to the said demand, nor did it give any answer to any of the request the opposite party tabled. Because of the existence of an arbitration clause in the agreement, the opposite party through a lawyer, transmitted a notice dated 18.8.91 asking the petitioner to appoint an arbitrator, but to no avail. In the wake of the said passive stance of the petitioner, the opposite party felt that a specific dispute had emerged between himself and the petitioner for which an arbitrator was required to be appointed. The opposite party, hence, instituted the said arbitration miscellaneous case seeking appointment of an arbitrator. 

 4. The petitioner recorded its appearance in the said Miscellaneous case as the opposite party and made endeavor to repel the opposite party's allegation by filling written objection, denying most of the factual allegations and claims, particularly the claim that the work had been completed, while admitting the factum of the agreement;. The pivotal thrust of the petitioners objection, however, was erected on the assertion that there existed no scope for the appointment of an arbitration under clause 28 of the contract, in so far as the opposite party had not brought entire work to a competition, but left 26% of the same undone. 

 5. After hearing the parties, he learned court below allowed the said arbitration miscellaneous case and directed the respective parties to provide with the names of Arbitrator within 1.11.2001 , which order aggrieved the petitioner and hence, this civil revisional application. 

 7. Mr. Ahmed also took us though the Exbt. "D" Series in support the factual assertion that no more than 74% of the Work was completed Citing a decision of this Division, promulgated, in the case British Airways plc. V. Bangladesh Air Services Pvt. Ltd. Reported in 48 DLR(HC) 249, Mr. Ahmed submitted that the said decision stands for the proposition that the power of the Arbitration court under section 8 of the Arbitration Act of 1940 (Act X of 1940), was very limited indeed and is circumscribe by the terms of the contract itself. He concluded by submitting that the learned court below acted beyond his jurisdiction by making the impugned order. 

 10. Perusal of clause 28 leads us to the equation that the determination of this appeal is dependant on the resolution of two issues of a twined nature, both couched upon the moot question of jurisdiction of the learned court below namely. whether, (1) in view of the General Managers exclusive power to appoint arbitrator, the court can act as an alter ego of the said designated functionary, (2) in view of the proviso to the said clause 28, which contemplates completion or abandonment of the work, it was open to the learned court below to assume jurisdiction to appoint an arbitrator, Section 8 of the said Act, which is, beyond dichotomy, the only available legislative scheme, runs, power of court of appoint arbitrator or umpire(1) In any of the following cases 

 (b)	If any appointment arbitrator or umpire neglects or refused to act, or is incapable of acting or dies, and the arbitration agreement does not show that it was intended that the vacancy should not be supplied and the parties or the arbitrators, as the case may be do not supply the vacancy or. 

 Any party may serve the other parties or the arbitrators as the case maybe with a written notice to concur in the appointment or appointments or in supplying the vacancy. 

 (2) If the appointment is not made within fifteen clear days after the service of the said notice. the court may, on the application of the party who gave the notice and after giving the other parties an opportunity of being heard, appoint an arbitrator or arbitrator or umpire, as the case may be who shall have like power to act in the reference and to make an award as if he or they had been appointed by consent of parties." 

 11. It is as clear as wedgewood blue that the court can, act under section 8(1) (a), only where in arbitration clause Makes the arbitrators appointment dependent upon the co sensuality of the parties. The Lahore High Court in Anjuman I Ahmadiya Ashait-1 Islam Lahore Vs. Ghulam ahmed (Rahman. J), DLR (Lah) 98 held that section 8 deals ...with Cases where appointment of arbitrator is to be by the consent of all the parties. The Karachi High Court in Intertrade Ltd. V. Trading Corporation of Pakistan Ltd. (Zaffar Hussain, J) PLD 1976 Kar 496 said that under the Arbitration Act agreement of parties has a sanctity which cannot be violated and that section 8 does not confer authority on the court to substitute 'the original agreement by an entirely new one. 

 12. In the present case, the agreement leaves no room for the confluence of the parties in appointing arbitrator but confers un-conjoined power of appointment on the General Manager of the petitioner. It is, therefore, incommensurable with the contention that section g (1)(a) which can play its part only where the appointment is dependent on the concurrence of the parties could be invoked by the opposite party. It the said sub section was not capable of being taken in aid the learned judge belows decision was obviously ultravires the Arbitration Act. 

 13. We are well aware of the decision arrived at by the Dhaka High Court in the case of Chief Engineer pak PWD Karachi V Sami and Co and others 22 DLR (DHAKA) 702 where, it was observed. The last point urged by the learned Additional Attorney General is that the arbitration agreement stipulated that the arbitrator was to be appointed by the Chief Engineer, Pakistan public work Department and as such the court had no jurisdiction to appoint an arbitrator under section 8 of the Arbitration Act. It cannot be said that when the arbitrator nominated by the Chief Engineer Pakistan public works Department refuses to function as an arbitrator and when the petitioner fails to appoint a subsequent arbitrator in agreement with the opposite party No. 1 within the statutory period. Even then the court does not have any power under section 8 of the Arbitration Act, we are of the view that the power and the jurisdiction conferred on the court under section 8 of the Arbitration Act was not intended to be taken away by such a clause in the Arbitration agreement. But that was a case where sub section (1) (b) of section rather than (1) (a) of the said section was the pertinent one, because in that case, an arbitrator was previously appointed by the designated incumbent but the arbitrator subsequently declined to carry on as such and hence, sub section (1)(b) of section 8 was beyond any qualm, applicable, whereas sub section (1) (h) has no role play in the instant case as it is entirely dependent on section 8(1)(a). The principle enunciated in pak P.WD„ case, is therefore out of the instant cases context. 

 15. The Rule that an arbitration clause is invariably dependent on the unanimity of the parties, necessary lead to the corollary that the parties are left with free hands to decide the ambit and extent of arbitrable disputes as well as the for location, applicable legal regime and procedure to be adopted. What sort of disputes whether all or some or any particular type shall be referred to Arbitration whether the arbitration agreement shall be an absolute one or be circumscribed by any rider depends on the sweet will of the parties? This is one notable area of the law of contract where the doctrine of freedom of contract is allowed its fullest classicism As viscount simon L.C. observed, the language of the arbitration clause in the contract can be as broad as can well be imagined (Heyman V. Darwins Ltd. 1942 AC 356), This view about virtually unclotted freedom and the view that power conferred by section 8 of the Act X 1940 stems from the agreement of the parties and that the court cannot go beyond what the parties agreed to received generous support from the decision in the case of British Airways ple V. Bangladesh Air Services pvt. Ltd. supra (Subsequently left un disturbed by the Appellate Division.) 

 17. Where the arbitration agreement is an untrammeled one here could hardly be any impediment on the courts competence in appointing an arbitrator, But it would be paralogistic to hold that when an arbitration clause contains an abstente, as in the present one, the court could assume jurisdiction when such riders remain unfulfilled. It is nobody’s case that persons designate issued the necessary certificate. In this case there exists divergence of claims between the parties on the question of completion. But when both the parties to the agreement by their own volition, equipped the General Manager with the exclusive authority to issue completion certificate, the court, exercising power -under section 8(1)(a), has title to do when the described certificate is not forthcoming Completion or abandonment of work being the key to unlock the arbitration clause and the General Manager being reposed with the singular authority to certify completion. It was certainly beyond the competence of the learned court below to proceed to act under the authority of section 8(1)(a) while the General Manager remained mum, even if, ignominiously, as Mr. Islam complained. 

 18. Mr. Islams fright that the presence of the arbitration clause would clong his passage to a civil court action reflects embroilment. It shall go without saying that if for whatever reason the arbitration. Clause, cannot take off, nothing would empower a civil 'court from staying civil proceedings simply because section 34 of the Act X of 1940 would not in such a case, apply. There would be nothing to pull back the opposite party, should he wish to pursue an action for quantum meruit either. In any event, while clause 28 prefulgen contains an abstente, excluding decisions which require certificate, from the purview of the arbitration clause nothing would prevent the opposite party from pursuing civil action in respect to such a matter, as the present matter, as the present matter in dispute is which comes under the said exclusionary zone. 

 20. This revisional petition, being therefore, deservant of accomplishment, is allowed hereby wherefore the impugned order dated 18.10.2001 passed by the learned 3rd sub ordinate Judge. Dhaka, in Arbitration Miscellaneous case no. 41 of 1999 is set aside. The aforementioned rule is consequently made absolute without any order as to cost.
